children: Central banks under Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will start paying "lip service" to broad money supply metrics, but this mini-monetarist revival is ultimately a "fade" that won't alter near-term interest rate
paths or significantly affect asset prices
, according to TS Lombard's Dario Perkins.

The shift marks a return to something resembling the late 1990s, when central banks paid attention to monetary aggregates but didn't let the data sway short-term policy decisions—and there was certainly no attempt to target specific metrics, Perkins pointed out in a recent note.

For European Central Bank and Bank of England watchers, this represents familiar territory, as European officials were once comfortable using monetary language. For Fed watchers, the adjustment will be more pronounced: the Fed will need to resume publishing broader monetary metrics and may even reference them in official publications, Perkins said.

Meanwhile, speculation that Warsh's focus on quantities rather than prices will involve aggressively shrinking the Fed's balance sheet is overblown, Perkins argued. The notion that quantitative tightening could justify lower interest rates doesn't hold up given the fuzzy link between QT, broad money, and inflation.

While Fed officials including Michelle Bowman and Lorie Logan have expressed interest in returning to the pre-2008 operating system based on reserve scarcity, there is currently no Federal Open Market Committee consensus for shrinking the balance sheet. Warsh is unlikely to pursue anything that threatens financial stability shortly after assuming office, Perkins noted, contending that if aggressive QT does materialize, it would likely be paired with bank deregulation, making it friendlier to risk assets.

"And while the Fed chair has recently appointed a new taskforce to study the issue, we thinkit will focus on reforms designed to stop the balance sheet blowing out permanently in the futurerather than recommend immediate asset sales," the note said.

The monetarist revival reflects policymakers fighting the last war. Monetarist-leaning economists correctly warned of post-COVID inflation when the consensus couldn't imagine such an outcome. But those same analysts were soon misled by unstable velocity: when money supply contracted after central banks raised rates and shrank balance sheets, many predicted severe downturns that never materialized. British economist Tim Congdon warned of a deflationary trap, while Steve Hanke of Johns Hopkins forecast "one whopper of a recession in 2023." Both were wrong, Perkins said, demonstrating that tracking the money supply is no panacea for macro forecasting.
